newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S., Japan shift focus to strategic issues.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Japan shift focus to strategic issues.

text.p: With a deal to cut back U.S. bases behind them, Japan and the United States are focusing on new defence issues, including how much Tokyo can help in a regional conflict and assist in developing a high-tech system to shoot down missiles.

The deal to cut back bases in the southern prefecture of Okinawa was announced on Monday by U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry, U.S. Ambassador to Japan Walter Mondale, Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda and Defence Minister Fumio Kyuma.
They said the focus was now shifting to strategic issues that include updating a set of guidelines under the 1960 U.S.-Japan Security Treaty.

Japan's constitution bans the state from joining collective security arrangements or offensive alliances. That means Japan cannot send its military to help U.S. forces in an armed conflict, unless Japan itself is invaded.
Washington wants Japan to commit itself to much more than that, especially in the event of a future armed conflict in the region, such as with Stalinist North Korea.
Washington also wants Tokyo's cooperation in multilateral peacekeeping and disaster relief operations.

"This means Japan is gradually moving from playing a pure supplementary security role to that of a full-fledged partner," said military analyst Haruo Fujii. "What will happen if the Taiwan Strait incident happened again?"
In March, the U.S. Navy dispatched two aircraft carrier battle groups to waters around Taiwan after China test-fired missiles near the island during Taiwan's presidential elections.
Japanese leaders are quietly behind an expansion of the country's dormant military role but due to political concerns have to tread softly, analysts say.
It remains to be seen if the Japanese navy, one of the strongest in the world in terms of conventional arms, could stand by and watch its U.S. allies fight alone in a future regional conflict.
So the pressure is now on Japan to define what it can do within the constitutional framework, such as providing supply operations in wartime, Fujii and other analysts said.
Washington also wants Japanese involvement in developing a satellite-and-ground missile system that can detect and destroy an incoming ballistic missile, called Theatre Missile Defence (TMD).
"Washington is especially looking for Japanese funds and high technology," Fujii said.
For two years, Japan's defence ministry has conducted limited feasibility studies for the TMD, but the Japanese government has so far refused to give it a full go-ahead.
After Monday's talks, Ikeda and Kyuma declared that the agreement to streamline U.S. bases on Okinawa was a watershed.

The four officials signed an agreement to return a fifth of the land taken up by U.S. military facilities on Okinawa, a deal designed to quell public anger against concentrated U.S. military presence on the tiny East China Sea island.

But many Okinawans were disappointed by Monday's agreement because it did not reduce the 28,000 U.S. troop strength there and the land would be freed on condition that the facilities in question will be moved to other bases on Okinawa.
